draft.title: The tri-component model of attitudes
card: An attitude is a lasting way of thinking and feeling about a person, object, group or issue. The tri-component model says an attitude has three parts.
how you feel about the target, such as liking it, fearing it or being disgusted by it.
how you act, or intend to act, toward the target, such as buying it, avoiding it or speaking up for it.
what you believe or know about the target, such as thinking it is healthy or unsafe. The three parts can disagree, so a person may believe one thing and act in another way.
draft.remember: An attitude is made of feelings, actions and beliefs, and these parts may not match.

a.q: Priya says, "I think fast food is bad for my health." Which part of her attitude is this?
opts: Cognitive, because it is a belief about fast food
Affective, because it is a feeling about fast food
Behavioural, because it is a way of acting toward it
Affective, because it is a judgement about her health
a.why: Thinking that fast food is bad for health is a belief about it, so it is the cognitive part. It is not the affective part, because she has not said how she feels, such as enjoying or disliking it.
a.clue: Is she stating a belief, a feeling or an action?

b.q: Tom believes recycling helps the environment and says he feels proud when he recycles. He rarely sorts his rubbish at home. What does this show about his attitude?
opts: His actions clash with his beliefs and feelings
His beliefs clash with his feelings and actions
His feelings clash with his beliefs and actions
His parts all match, so he has no attitude to recycling
b.why: Tom's belief and his pride in recycling agree with each other, but his rarely sorting rubbish does not match them. So the behavioural part disagrees with the other two. The parts of an attitude can disagree, so he still has an attitude.
b.clue: Sort Tom's belief, feeling and action. Which one differs?

a.best: Cognitive, because it is a belief about fast food

b.best: His actions clash with his beliefs and feelings
